# dbd — Database Designer (Full Reference)

> A standalone CLI and embeddable Rust library for managing database schemas as code.

## What is dbd?

dbd manages database schemas as code. You write SQL DDL files, organize them in folders, and dbd handles dependency ordering, migrations, data loading, documentation, and deployment.

It is:
- A single binary with zero runtime dependencies
- An embeddable library (`dbd-core` crate) for Rust apps
- Multi-target: PostgreSQL, Supabase, SQLite, Convex from the same source
- Migration-aware with versioned snapshots and auto-generated ALTER scripts
- Safe with database-side environment guards

---

## Project structure

```
myproject/
  design.yaml          # Project config
  ddl/                 # SQL files (auto-discovered)
    table/config/
      lookups.ddl
      lookup_values.ddl
    view/config/
      genders.ddl
    materialized_view/analytics/
      daily_sales.ddl
    enum/config/
      status.sql
    sequence/config/
      ticket_no.ddl
    procedure/staging/
      import_lookups.ddl
    role/
      admin.ddl
  import/              # Staging data
    staging/
      lookups.csv
    dev/staging/       # Dev-only data
      fixtures.csv
  policies/            # RLS policies
    config/
      lookups.sql
  snapshots/           # Auto-generated
  migrations/          # Auto-generated
  export/              # Auto-generated
```

### File path → entity name

| Path | Entity name | Type |
|------|-------------|------|
| `ddl/table/config/lookups.ddl` | `config.lookups` | table |
| `ddl/view/config/genders.ddl` | `config.genders` | view |
| `ddl/procedure/staging/import_lookups.ddl` | `staging.import_lookups` | procedure |
| `ddl/function/config/get_user.ddl` | `config.get_user` | function |
| `ddl/enum/config/status.sql` | `config.status` | enum |
| `ddl/materialized_view/analytics/daily_sales.ddl` | `analytics.daily_sales` | materialized view |
| `ddl/sequence/config/ticket_no.ddl` | `config.ticket_no` | sequence |
| `ddl/role/admin.ddl` | `admin` | role |

Schema-scoped types: `ddl/<type>/<schema>/<name>.<ext>`
Non-schema types: `ddl/<type>/<name>.<ext>`

`<type>` ∈ `table` | `view` | `materialized_view` | `function` | `procedure` | `enum` | `sequence` | `role` (`matview` is accepted for `materialized_view`). Extensions: `.ddl` or `.sql`. There is no `trigger` folder. **Singular is canonical**; the plural folder name (`functions/`, `tables/`, …) is accepted but `dbd doctor --fix` migrates plural → singular (merging into an existing singular folder; on a same-name collision the newer file is kept and the older saved as `<name>.ddl.bkp`).

---

## design.yaml

### Minimal example

```yaml
project:
  name: MyProject

source:
  dialect: postgresql

target:
  postgres:
    url: $DATABASE_URL

schemas: [config, staging]
```

### Full example

```yaml
project:
  name: MyProject
  note: E-commerce database schema

source:
  dialect: postgresql

target:                              # ONLY the first entry is read
  supabase:                          # same Postgres adapter; the key adds Supabase rules
    url: $DATABASE_URL
    skip_schemas: [auth, storage]      # Supabase owns these — dbd won't manage their entities
    extensions:
      - uuid-ossp
      - name: postgis
        schema: extensions
    roles:
      - name: advanced
        refers: [basic]
      - name: basic
    grants:                            # any target key; merged with schemas[].grants
      config:
        anon: [usage, select]
        service_role: [usage, all]

  # Other targets — use ONE of these as the first entry instead:
  # postgres: { url: $DATABASE_URL }
  # sqlite:   { url: sqlite://./local.db }    # or sqlite::memory:, file:/abs/path.db
  # convex:   { url: convex: }                # writes ./convex/schema.ts; convex://./out?deploy=true

schemas:
  - config:
      exposed: true                    # PostgREST serves it → inspect reports tables with no RLS policy
  - staging:
      grants:
        app_user: [usage, select]
  - extensions

external:
  - name: auth.users                   # only `name` is read
    note: Supabase managed auth table

apply:                          # lifecycle hooks around the DDL phase
  before:
    - sql/pre_ddl.sql           # after design+scope checks, before the first entity
  after:
    - sql/realtime.sql          # after every entity + matview stamp, BEFORE policies/
    - script: sql/grants.sql    # declare tables dbd cannot derive by parsing
      writes: [app.messages]

import:                         # files found by convention; this only tunes the load
  options:
    truncate: true
    null_value: ''
  tables:                       # per-table overrides — not an allowlist
    - staging.lookup_values:
        truncate: false
  after:
    - import/loader.sql         # runs on `dbd import` and `dbd deploy` — NOT on `dbd apply`

export:
  - config.lookups
  - config.lookup_values:
      format: jsonl

materialized_views:             # pg_cron refresh scheduling for ddl/materialized_view/ entities
  options:
    refresh: "0 2 * * *"        # shared cron schedule (omit ⇒ no scheduled refresh)
    concurrently: true          # REFRESH … CONCURRENTLY needs a unique index on the matview
  overrides:                    # per-matview overlay onto options (by qualified name)
    analytics.top_products: { refresh: "*/30 * * * *" }

dbml:
  base:
    exclude:
      schemas: [staging, extensions]
    auto_group_by_schema: true
  core:
    include:
      schemas: [config]
    output: core.dbml
    groups:
      - name: lookups
        tables: [config.lookups, config.lookup_values]

scopes:                         # named entity selections (deploy a subset)
  hub:
    includes: [config, app.users]   # whole schema OR specific entity
    deps: report                    # report (default) | include
  reporting:
    excludes: [staging, app.audit_log]
  everything: all                   # bare `all` = the full set

ignore:
  - bfs
  - my_company.*

format:
  keyword_case: lower
  query_style: river
```

Parsed but never read — reserved, change nothing: `import.staging`,
`import.options.format`, `import.tables[].env`, `target.schemas`, `target.path`,
`external[].columns`, `external[].note` (documentation only). Only the first
`target:` entry is read; a second one is ignored.

### Section reference

| Section | Purpose | Required |
|---------|---------|----------|
| `project` | Name, note, version, `released` | yes |
| `source` | DDL file dialect (default: postgresql) | no |
| `target` | Deploy targets with connection + target-specific config | yes |
| `schemas` | Schema declarations (universal) | yes |
| `external` | FK stubs for external tables | no |
| `apply` | Lifecycle hooks `before`/`after` | no |
| `import` | Data import tuning (options, per-table overrides, after scripts) | no |
| `export` | Tables to export (empty ⇒ all tables) | no |
| `materialized_views` | pg_cron refresh scheduling | no |
| `dbml` | DBML generation filters | no |
| `scopes` | Named entity selections for subset deploys | no |
| `ignore` | Reference classification overrides | no |
| `format` | DDL formatter options (see `dbd format`) | no |

### Universal vs target-specific config

| Universal (top-level) | Target-specific |
|---|---|
| `schemas` (+ `grants`, `exposed` per entry) | `extensions` (Postgres/Supabase) |
| `external` | `roles` (Postgres/Supabase) |
| `import` / `export` | `grants` (any target key; Postgres grant model) |
| `dbml` / `scopes` | `url` (connection / output) |
| `ignore` / `format` | `skip_schemas` (leave a target's own schemas unmanaged) |

`project.released` is set by `dbd release` only. `dbd reconcile` refuses when it
is `true` and checks nothing else.

### Scopes — subset deploys from one design

A **scope** is a named selection of entities, letting one `design.yaml` deploy
to more than one database (e.g. a full primary DB and a smaller embedded-Postgres
hub). Scopes are orthogonal to `target` (the DB platform/dialect) and to the
connection — you pair a scope with a database at run time:

```sh
dbd deploy --scope hub --database $HUB_URL
```

- Each scope has `includes:` and/or `excludes:`, each item being one of:
  **a bare schema** (`config` — all its entities plus the `CREATE SCHEMA` entity),
  **a qualified entity** (`app.users`), or **a `schema.*` wildcard** (every entity
  under the schema, same `prefix.*` syntax as the `ignore:` list). The wildcard
  does NOT carry the schema entity, so `excludes: [staging.*]` drops staging's
  tables but keeps the `staging` schema, while `excludes: [staging]` drops the
  schema too; for `includes`, `schema.*` and `schema` are equivalent. An unknown
  name or wildcard prefix that matches nothing is an error (typo protection).
  Empty `includes` ⇒ start from the full set; `excludes` removes.
- `deps: report | include` (default `report`):
  - `report` — a **dependency gap** (an in-scope entity referencing a managed
    entity outside the scope) is an error. `dbd inspect --scope X` lists the gaps
    with their dependency chain and exits non-zero; `apply`/`import`/`deploy`
    refuse (including `--dry-run`).
  - `include` — the working set auto-expands to the transitive dependency
    closure before the command runs (every scope-aware command, not just
    `deploy`).
- A reference to an `external:` entity is never a gap — `external:` is the only
  "satisfied elsewhere" mechanism (there is no "ignore gaps" mode).
- `extensions: [..]` — optional per-scope extension allowlist. Omitted ⇒ all
  `target.extensions` apply (default); a list ⇒ only those; `[]` ⇒ none. Lets a
  scope deploy to a DB lacking an extension (e.g. embedded PG without pgvector).
  Name extensions by bare name (`vector`, `postgis`); roles/externals stay
  always-on regardless.
- Omit `default` (or the whole `scopes:` block) ⇒ the full set is used. Define a
  `default:` scope only if a bare `dbd deploy` (no `--scope`) should itself
  deploy a subset. `all` and `default` are reserved: `--scope all` is always the
  full set (a scope you name `all` is unreachable), and a run without `--scope`
  uses `default` when defined — and is pinned as `default`. A scope's value may
  be the bare string `all`.
- Gaps come from recorded references (FKs; view/routine reads, writes, calls).
  A column typed with an out-of-scope enum is NOT detected as a gap in 0.24.1 —
  include the enum's schema yourself.
- Per-scope migrations fall out automatically: pending-migration steps for
  out-of-scope entities are skipped while the per-database version still advances.
  A table removed from the design is in no named scope's working set, so its
  drop step never runs under a named scope.

`snapshot`, `release` and `migrate` deliberately ignore `--scope` and warn when
given it. A snapshot records the *design*, not one database: a scoped baseline
would omit entities, and every later `dbd snapshot` would diff against an
incomplete record and emit a spurious `CREATE` for them on every plane. Scope
decides which migration steps *run*, not which ones exist — `dbd deploy --scope
daemon` on a released project applies only the in-scope migrations while the
database's version still advances.

Scopes are honored by every entity-selecting command. **Gap-gated** (filter, and
refuse on a gap under `deps: report`, `--dry-run` included): `inspect`, `apply`,
`import`, `deploy`, `reconcile`, `diff`. **Filter-only**: `dbml`, `combine`,
`emit`, `graph`, `diagram`, `export`, `refresh`, `policies`, `reset` —
`inspect --scope` is where gaps surface. **Ignored with a warning**: `snapshot`,
`release`, `migrate`, `doctor`, `init`, `merge`, `format`, `install`. Unfiltered
paths: `import -n X -f file`, `policies --dry-run` and `deploy --dry-run`'s policy
count. `dbml`/`combine` emit external stub tables for out-of-scope FK
targets (and `combine` keeps roles + the scope's allowed extensions); `reset` is
entity-level (drops the scope's own objects individually; `--schemas` additionally
restricts the dropped schemas to those the scope occupies, roles dropped only on a
full reset). The shared primitive is
`Design::scoped_entities(&ResolvedScope) -> Result<Vec<Entity>>` (closure under `include`,
plain set under `report`, everything for the all-scope).

**A scope narrows what is applied, not what the project owns.** Under a scope,
`reconcile` and `diff` hide what the design declares outside the scope from the
live side, so it is neither altered nor pruned. Before 0.24.1 a scoped
`reconcile --prune` dropped such tables (#40) — upgrade before running one.

Policies are scope-filtered too: a file's target is read from its path
(`policies/<schema>/<table>.sql`), and a policy whose table is outside the
working set is skipped and reported rather than run. A file off that layout has
no derivable target and always applies.

### Lifecycle hooks (`apply.before` / `apply.after` / `import.after`)

SQL dbd does not model — attaching a table to a publication (Supabase realtime),
`grant`s, other post-DDL setup.

| Hook | Runs on | Position |
|---|---|---|
| `apply.before` | `apply` **and** `deploy` | after design+scope checks, before the first entity |
| `apply.after` | `apply` **and** `deploy` | after every entity applied + matview stamped, **before** the configured grants and `policies/` |
| `import.after` | `import` **and** `deploy` | after the data load and the import procedures |

**`import.after` never runs on `dbd apply`.** Only `dbd import` and `dbd deploy`
reach the import phase (and `import -n X -f file` skips it). Post-DDL SQL parked
there — often because it was once the only hook available — silently does
nothing on `dbd apply`. If the hook's job is
"run once every entity exists", it belongs in `apply.after`.

`apply.after` runs before `policies/` because publications and grants attach to
objects that must already exist, while RLS policies are independent of them. A
hook that needs a policy to exist will not find one.

**Entry format.** A project-relative path, or `{script: <path>, writes: [tables]}`.
Scripts run in list order. A path dbd cannot find is an **error, not a skip**.
`..` and absolute paths are refused.

**Scope filtering.** A hook runs only when every table it depends on is in the
working set — the same rule as staging entries. Otherwise it is skipped and
reported, and the run continues:

```
⚠ after-script import/loader.sql skipped — needs staging.values, which is outside scope 'partial'
```

**When `writes:` is required.** dbd derives a script's tables by parsing it,
which works only when they appear as SQL identifiers. A realtime-publication
hook names its tables as *data* — inside `array['a','b']` and
`format('alter publication … %I', t)` — where `select_tables()`/`dml_tables()`
return empty. No parser can recover those; declare them with `writes:`.

A script with no derivable dependencies and no `writes:` **always runs**. That
is the safe direction (silently skipping a hook because analysis came up short
would hide, say, a realtime hook quietly not firing), but it means scope
filtering is a correctness aid, **not a security boundary** — never use a scope
to prevent a hook from running.

---

## Commands

### Global options

| Option | Short | Default | Description |
|--------|-------|---------|-------------|
| `--config` | `-c` | `design.yaml` | Config file name, inside the `--source` directory |
| `--database` | `-d` | `$DATABASE_URL` | Database URL (overrides config) |
| `--environment` | `-e` | `prod` | `dev` or `prod`; `development`/`production` accepted as aliases, anything else is an error. Selects `import/<env>/`, recorded in bookkeeping (the reset guard reads it) |
| `--source` | `-s` | `.` | Project directory; `dbd deploy` also accepts a GitHub repo |
| `--verbose` | `-v` | | Verbose output (show all details) |
| `--scope` | | full set | Scope name from design.yaml (entity subset) |
| `--deps` | | scope's own | Gap policy override: `report` or `include` |

The adapter (PostgreSQL/SQLite/Convex) is chosen from the connection **URL scheme**, not a target name (`mysql://`/`sqlserver://` are refused by name — there is no MySQL or SQL Server adapter); the first `target.<name>` block in design.yaml supplies the platform config and default `url`. There is no target-name selector — override the connection per run with `-d`/`$DATABASE_URL` (pair with `--scope` for multi-database deploys).

### dbd init

`-t`/`--target` here is the **platform** to scaffold (`postgres` | `supabase`), not a design.yaml target name.

```sh
dbd init -n myproject
dbd init -n myproject --target supabase
```

The scaffold: `design.yaml`, `ddl/{table,view,materialized_view,function,procedure,enum}/`,
`ddl/table/public/example.ddl`, `import/`. `--target supabase` adds a `config` schema,
`external:` entries (`auth.users`, `auth.uid`, `storage.objects`, `storage.buckets`) and
`ignore:` patterns — no grants.

**Reverse-engineer.** `dbd init --from-db <conn>` (or `$DATABASE_URL`/`-d` when no value) and
`dbd init --from-dbml <file>` generate the whole project from an existing source instead of the
sample scaffold: introspect → reconstruct canonical DDL → write `design.yaml` + the
`ddl/<kind>/<schema>/<name>.ddl` tree, then emit a **baseline snapshot at `--version`** (default 1)
so the project lands version-tracked. `--from-db` and `--from-dbml` are mutually exclusive.

```sh
dbd init --from-db postgres://user:pass@host/db   # new project from a live Postgres DB
dbd init --from-db sqlite://./app.db              # …or a SQLite database (file:/sqlite:: too)
dbd init --from-db                                # connection from -d / $DATABASE_URL
dbd init --from-dbml schema.dbml                  # from a DBML file (no connection)
dbd init --from-db $DATABASE_URL --version 3      # base project.version + baseline snapshot version
dbd init --from-db ... --schema config --schema staging   # allowlist (repeatable)
dbd init --from-db ... --exclude-schema audit             # drop a schema (repeatable)
dbd init --from-db ... --all-schemas              # include Supabase platform schemas
dbd init --from-db ... --roles                    # also reverse-engineer cluster-global roles
dbd init --from-db ... --dry-run                  # print the plan, write nothing
```

Flags: `--name` (default = DB name), `--version N` (base `project.version` + baseline snapshot
version, default 1), `--schema`/`--exclude-schema` (repeatable allow/deny), `--all-schemas`
(bypass the Supabase platform denylist; Postgres internals always excluded), `--roles` (opt-in
roles — DBML has none, so a no-op there), `--dry-run`. Postgres internals (`pg_catalog`,
`information_schema`, `pg_temp*`, `pg_toast*`) are always excluded; on Supabase, platform schemas
(`auth`, `storage`, `realtime`, `extensions`, `graphql*`, `vault`, `pgsodium*`, `supabase_*`,
`cron`, `net`, …) are excluded unless `--all-schemas`.

The target **dialect is taken from the connection URL scheme** (`postgres://` → `postgres`
target; `sqlite://`/`file:`/`sqlite::memory:` → `sqlite` target); `--target` is ignored with
`--from-db`, and `--from-dbml` accepts only the default `postgres`. A Supabase database
lands as a `postgres` target — rename the key to `supabase` for Supabase's rules. The
baseline snapshot does not set `project.released`. **SQLite** is captured verbatim
from `sqlite_master` — tables (CHECK, type affinity, AUTOINCREMENT, WITHOUT ROWID), user indexes,
and views, losslessly; no schemas/enums/functions/sequences/roles, **triggers skipped**; files are
flat (`ddl/table/<name>.ddl`) and `design.yaml` carries `schemas: []`. (`dbd inspect` on a SQLite
project may emit benign schema-qualification warnings; the DDL is valid and applies.)

`init --from-db` **refuses** to run against a **dbd-managed** database (`dbd.meta`, or a legacy
`_dbd_meta`, in any schema → use `dbd merge`), and refuses in a directory that already has a
`design.yaml` (use `merge`). The
generated `design.yaml` writes the connection as the literal `$DATABASE_URL` env reference —
**secrets never land in the repo**.

### dbd merge

Sync a database (or `--from-dbml <file>`) into the **current** project — same introspection and
emitter as `init --from-db`, but never creates or edits `design.yaml`.

```sh
dbd merge postgres://user:pass@host/db   # sync into the current project
dbd merge                                # connection from -d / $DATABASE_URL
dbd merge --from-dbml schema.dbml        # sync from a DBML file (no connection)
dbd merge --dry-run                      # preview the plan + the snapshot version
dbd merge --schema config --exclude-schema audit   # same selection flags as init
dbd merge --roles                        # also reverse-engineer roles (opt-in)
```

Every merge that proceeds **overwrites the introspected DDL into the project (no `.bak`)** and
**captures the delta as a new snapshot version** (a baseline if the project had none), bumping
`design.yaml`'s `project.version`. Each generated file is classified: **created** (no file → written),
**unchanged** (byte-identical → untouched; runs through the same formatter as `dbd format`, so a
generated-then-formatted file stays unchanged), **conflict** (differs from the DB → replaced in place),
**orphan** (an existing managed `.ddl`/`.sql` with no matching DB entity — **reported, never
deleted**). `--dry-run` previews the plan + the snapshot version that would be created:
`[dry-run] N created · N unchanged · N conflict(s) (would overwrite, no .bak)`; a real run prints
`N file(s) written · snapshot vN created`. Like `init --from-db`, `merge` does not set
`project.released`.

`merge` requires an existing project (refuses if no `design.yaml` → use `init --from-db`). It never
edits config, so files written for a schema not in `schemas:` produce a **warning**. Secrets never
written (the connection is not persisted; `$DATABASE_URL`).

**Version safety.** When the target is a **dbd-managed** database (`dbd.meta`, or a legacy
`_dbd_meta`, exists), `merge` compares the DB's applied version **D** against the project version
**Y** (`0` when unset): **D < Y → refuse** (project is ahead of a stale DB; overwriting would
discard newer work — no override flag; `dbd apply` to advance the DB, or revert the project via
version control); **D ≥ Y, or any foreign DB / DBML source** → the overwrite + auto-snapshot path.
(A DBML or foreign source has no `dbd.meta`/`_dbd_meta`, so the gate never engages — it always
takes the snapshot path.)

### Reverse-engineering — entity coverage

Captured from a **live database** (`init --from-db` / `merge`): schemas, extensions, enums, tables
(columns, defaults, identity, PK/FK/unique/check constraints, indexes incl. `USING gin/gist/brin/hash`,
table + column comments, `serial`/identity columns reproduced through the column), views,
materialized views (definition + indexes from `pg_matviews`, written to `ddl/materialized_view/`),
functions
& procedures (full bodies, verbatim via `pg_get_functiondef`; overloads share one file;
extension-provided routines excluded), roles (opt-in `--roles`; cluster-global, name + memberships
only, never passwords; superusers/`pg_*`/cloud/Supabase platform roles filtered), and standalone
sequences (`ddl/sequence/<schema>/<name>.ddl`).

**Not captured:** partial indexes (`… WHERE …`), expression indexes (`lower(name)`), triggers,
aggregates, operators, domains, composite types. dbd's own bookkeeping — the `dbd` schema
(`dbd.meta`/`dbd.migrations`) on Postgres/Supabase — is always excluded. Column order reflects the
DB's physical order — run `dbd format` to normalize.

A **DBML source** (`--from-dbml`) covers only **schemas + enums + tables + foreign keys** — DBML
cannot express functions, procedures, views, standalone sequences, roles, or check constraints.
`serial`/identity survive via the column.

### dbd inspect

```sh
dbd inspect
dbd inspect -n config.lookups
dbd inspect --verbose
dbd inspect --fix              # auto-format DDL files in place while validating
dbd inspect --scope hub        # report dependency gaps for a scope (exit 1 under report policy)
```

On a Postgres/Supabase project, `inspect` also prints an advisory **`Suggestions:`** section for
`CHECK` constraints that pin a column to a fixed set of string literals (`col IN ('a','b')`,
`= ANY(ARRAY[…])`, or an `OR`-chain of `col = '…'`) — better modeled as a Postgres `enum`. Advisory
only: never an error, never affects the exit code.

Columns sharing a value set become one proposal. Where the plain column name would name two different files, the type is named `<table>_<column>` instead (and `_2`, `_3` if that still collides) — the footer says how many were renamed and why. An identifier that is not a single ordinary path segment gets no path at all, just the candidate; likewise values needing escaping are printed unquoted and flagged, since escaped text is not the literal it came from.

**RLS report.** For every exposed schema (`exposed: true`, or `public` on a
`supabase` target), `inspect` lists tables with no `policies/<schema>/<table>.sql`
— advisory, never the exit code.

**Exit code (changed in v0.12.0).** `inspect` exits **1** when the design carries
a blocking error, 0 otherwise. It previously always exited 0, so a CI step
running `dbd inspect` passed green on a file `dbd apply` refuses — while apply's
own error said "run `dbd inspect` for the full report". Warnings and suggestions
never affect the exit code.

**Parse errors name their consequence.** A file dbd cannot parse is dropped from
the desired set, so a run would build a database missing that object;
`apply`/`reconcile`/`deploy` refuse instead. The report says so:

```
Errors:

./ddl/table/app/broken.ddl =>
  Parse error: Invalid statement: syntax error at or near ","

  → dbd apply / reconcile / deploy will refuse to run until these are fixed.
```

**Errors under `--scope`.** Only errors in the scope's working set block it, and
`inspect --scope` splits its report by the same rule the run uses — so `inspect`
and `apply` never disagree about what is broken. Out-of-scope errors are listed
under `Out of scope — not blocking '<scope>'` and do not affect the exit code,
but they are never suppressed: a file no scope builds is how a broken file
survives unnoticed. The summary's entity count is scope-aware.

### dbd apply

Applies all entities in dependency order. Handles pending migrations automatically.

```sh
dbd apply
dbd apply -n config.lookups
dbd apply --dry-run
```

Apply order is ONE dependency sort across all entity types. Each type has a band
it is never placed before — schema, extension, role, sequence, enum, table, view,
materialized view, function/procedure — and a real dependency can push an entity
later (a view calling a function goes after it; a function reading a view after
the view). Cyclic entities get an error and go last. Migrations interleave with
the tables they alter.

**Transaction.** On PostgreSQL the plan (entities, migrations, version stamp) runs
in ONE transaction; an interrupted upgrade rolls back. `apply.before` runs before
it; matview stamping, pg_cron sync and `apply.after` after it commits. Set
`DBD_NO_TX` (any value) for DDL that cannot run in a transaction (`CREATE INDEX
CONCURRENTLY`). SQLite applies without a transaction.

**Grants.** After the schema (entities, migrations, `apply.after`), `dbd apply`
applies the configured grants: `schemas[].grants` merged with the first target's
`grants` (target lists replace schema-entry lists per role). `usage` (lower case)
→ `GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA`; other perms → `GRANT … ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA` +
`ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES … ON TABLES`; then `NOTIFY pgrst, 'reload config'`. On a
`supabase` target, configured grants also give `anon`/`authenticated`/`service_role`
`USAGE` on every listed schema. Not under `--dry-run`, not filtered by `--scope`;
skipped with a note on SQLite/Convex. `--dry-run` lists entities only (no hooks,
no grants).

After entities apply, `dbd apply` (and `dbd deploy`) stamps a `dbd:hash` sentinel comment on any materialized view it just created and syncs pg_cron refresh jobs (`dbd:refresh:<schema>.<name>`) to match `materialized_views:` — see [dbd refresh](#dbd-refresh) and the `materialized_views` config. Matview DDL should be idempotent (`create materialized view if not exists …` + `create [unique] index if not exists …`).

**Scope guard.** Every successful `apply`/`deploy`/`reconcile` **pins** the database to the scope it applied, recorded in the bookkeeping table's `scope` column (`dbd.meta.scope` on Postgres/Supabase, `_dbd_meta.scope` on SQLite). A later `apply`/`deploy`/`reconcile`/`reset` that requests a *different* scope than the pin is refused ("scope guard: this database is pinned to scope 'X', but you requested 'Y'"), preventing a mistyped or forgotten `--scope` from building a divergent schema. Pass `--allow-scope-change` on the write command to re-point the database to the new scope (`reset --force` also bypasses). Databases created before this feature are unpinned and pin on their next write.

### dbd refresh

Runs `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW [CONCURRENTLY]` now, honoring each matview's resolved `concurrently`. `-n <entity>` or `-n <schema>.*` targets a subset; omit for all. For the initial populate or CI, independent of the pg_cron schedule. Recurring refresh is scheduled in-database via pg_cron (configured under `materialized_views:`). PostgreSQL/Supabase only.

```sh
dbd refresh
dbd refresh -n analytics.daily_sales
dbd refresh -n analytics.*
```

### dbd import

```sh
dbd import
dbd import -n staging.lookups
dbd import -n activity.hook_events -f ~/data/events.jsonl   # ad-hoc: load a specific file
dbd import --dry-run
dbd import -e dev
```

`-f`/`--file <path>` loads one explicit file into the `-n` table (required), format inferred
from the extension (.jsonl/.tsv/.csv), bypassing the `import/` convention. Symmetric note: on
`import` `-f` is the file; on `export` `-f` is the format. `dbd export -n <t> -f <fmt> -o <dir>`
writes `<dir>/<name>.<fmt>` (default `export/<schema>/<name>.<fmt>`) — `-o` lets export write
straight into the `import/` tree for a round-trip.

Execution: truncate → COPY data → call import procedures → run `import.after`.
CSV/TSV: the header row is skipped and columns load by position. `.json` files are
read as JSON Lines, like `.jsonl`; on PostgreSQL they go through
`staging.import_jsonb_to_table`, which dbd installs (creating `staging`). An import
procedure is any procedure/function that reads the staging table (body analysis,
not names; dynamic SQL is invisible); the plan is ordered by FK dependencies
between their write targets. `import.after` runs on every `dbd import` (with or
without `-n`) and on `dbd deploy`, never on `apply`; `-f` skips truncate,
procedures, `import.after` and scope. `import.tables` holds per-table overrides
(`truncate`, `format`, `null_value`) — it is not an allowlist.

Environment-specific data: files at `import/<schema>/file` load in every
environment; files at `import/<env>/<schema>/file` load only when `-e <env>`
matches. So `import/dev/staging/seed.csv` loads under `-e dev` but not `prod`.
Import procedures are matched to staging tables by reads/writes analysis, not by
naming convention.

### dbd export

```sh
dbd export
dbd export -n config.lookups
dbd export -n config.lookups -f jsonl
dbd export -o import/                 # write straight into the import/ tree
```

Reads table data out of the live database into files — the inverse of `import`.

`-n`/`--name <table>` exports one table. With no `export:` list in `design.yaml`,
every table (in scope) is exported; with one, only the listed tables — and `-n`
naming a table the list leaves out prints `No tables to export.` Only **tables**
are exported: a view under `export:` is skipped without a message. A per-entry
`format` wins over `-f`. `-f`/`--format <csv|tsv|jsonl>` selects
the format (default `csv`) — note the asymmetry with `import`, where `-f` is a
file path. `-o`/`--output <dir>` writes the selected tables flat as
`<dir>/<name>.<fmt>`; without it, files land at `export/<schema>/<name>.<fmt>`.

Pointing `-o` at `import/<schema>` produces a round-trip: what `export` writes,
`import` reads back under the `import/<schema>/<table>.<fmt>` convention (`-o` writes
`<table>.<fmt>` without the schema).

**Moving a long-lived system.** The pattern: views that dereference each FK back to
the natural key the import staging tables expect, listed under `export:`, so an
export from the old database matches the staging tables and an import into the new
one runs the same procedures as a fresh seed. In 0.24.1 `dbd export` skips views,
so export them with `psql "\copy (select * from <view>) to 'import/<schema>/<table>.csv'
with (format csv, header)"` until it can. Not needed when the import files are the
well-managed source of truth.

Per-table `export_data` is not available on Convex — `npx convex export` only
supports whole-deployment dumps, so the command errors with that explanation
rather than writing a partial file.

### dbd deploy

One-shot: fetch source → apply → grants → import → policies → cleanup.

`deploy` means "bring the database fully up from source", so RLS policies from
`policies/` are applied **unconditionally** — unlike `dbd apply`, where they are
opt-in behind `--with-policies`. Grants are the same `dbd apply` applies (schema +
target grants, the PostgREST ride-along on `supabase`), right after the schema and
before import and policies. `-c/--config` works as on every command.

`deploy` is the only command that accepts a GitHub source; every other command
refuses one with a message (clone the repo and pass its path). For a private
repository set `GITHUB_TOKEN` — sent as a bearer token to `api.github.com` only.
`--dry-run` checks the scope and counts data files and policy files (the policy
count is not scope-filtered).

```sh
dbd deploy --source sensei-hq/daemon/database -d $DATABASE_URL
dbd deploy --source sensei-hq/daemon/database@v2.1 -d $DATABASE_URL
dbd deploy --dry-run --source owner/repo/path -d $DATABASE_URL
dbd deploy --scope hub -d $HUB_URL          # deploy only the hub subset
dbd deploy --scope hub --deps include -d $HUB_URL   # auto-include dependencies
dbd deploy --no-cache --source owner/repo/path -d $URL     # re-download this source
dbd deploy --clear-cache --source owner/repo/path -d $URL  # wipe the whole cache first
```

GitHub sources are cached under `~/.cache/dbd` (macOS: `~/Library/Caches/dbd`).
`--no-cache` re-downloads the current source; `--clear-cache` removes the entire
cache directory before deploying. Both are no-ops for local path sources
(`--clear-cache` still clears the cache).

**Nothing is skipped silently.** Every phase reports its count, including zero,
and a deploy that imports nothing says why:

| Reason a data file did not load | Reported as |
| --- | --- |
| No `import/` directory | `no import/ directory — nothing to import` |
| File under `import/<other-env>/` | `N data file(s) under import/<env>/ skipped — this run's env is '<env>'` |
| Staging file failed to parse | `staging table X not imported — data file failed to parse` |
| Entry cut by `--scope` | `staging table X not imported — outside scope '<name>'` |
| `-n <name>` matched no staging file | `no staging data file matches --name <name>` |

A policy file that fails is **non-fatal**: it is reported as a warning, counted
in the summary (`N policy file(s) applied, M failed`), and the deploy still
exits 0. This is the wrong-`--env` trap — a deploy that applied DDL but seeded
no rows used to look indistinguishable from a clean success.

`dbd deploy` is a thin wrapper over the library's `Design::deploy`, so the CLI
and an embedding application run the identical pipeline and cannot drift.

### dbd reconcile

Pre-release (pre-v1) **declarative** apply: diff the live database against the
design and apply the difference in place — `CREATE` for new tables, `ALTER` for
changed ones — with **no snapshot files and no version bump**. This avoids
cutting a throwaway snapshot for every schema tweak while the design churns.

```sh
dbd reconcile --dry-run -d $DATABASE_URL              # preview the plan (entity summary)
dbd reconcile --dry-run -v -d $DATABASE_URL           # preview + show the column-level ALTER SQL
dbd reconcile -d $DATABASE_URL                        # apply (create + alter)
dbd reconcile --allow-destructive -d $DATABASE_URL    # also drop columns/constraints
dbd reconcile --prune -d $DATABASE_URL                # also drop orphaned tables
```

Add `-v` to a `--dry-run` to print the generated `ALTER` SQL beneath each altered
entity — the exact column-level change, before applying.

The diff is scoped to the schemas the design declares — reconcile never touches
tables in other schemas. Two kinds of destruction each need an explicit opt-in:
`--allow-destructive` drops a **column**/constraint from a managed table, or
removes an enum **value** (see below);
`--prune` drops a whole **orphaned table** (in a managed schema, no longer in the
design). Without `--prune`, orphans are reported and left in place. Under
`--scope`, a table the design declares outside the scope is never an orphan — a
scope narrows what is applied, not what the project owns (true from 0.24.1;
earlier releases dropped those tables under `--scope --prune`, #40). On a
`supabase` target Supabase's own schemas are never pruned. Orphaned
enums are only warned about, never auto-dropped. Reconcile is **disabled once the
project is released** (`project.released: true`) — see `dbd release`; it checks
that flag only.

Reconcile compares the introspected live schema against the design and
canonicalizes the two representations first: it lifts inline PK/UNIQUE to
structural constraints, schema-qualifies bare enum types (`status` →
`config.status`) to match introspection, and normalizes type aliases (`int4` →
`integer`, `timestamptz` → `timestamp with time zone`). It reconciles **columns**
(name/type/nullability/default/identity), **PK/UNIQUE** constraints, **foreign
keys**, **CHECK** constraints, **indexes** and **column comments**.

Everything is matched by shape, never by name — Postgres auto-names what the
design leaves unnamed, so a name difference is not drift. PK/UNIQUE match on their
columns, FKs on (columns, referenced table/columns, actions), CHECKs on the
canonicalized expression, indexes on (unique flag, access method, ordered
columns). A declared object the live DB lacks is added; one the design dropped is
removed (`DROP CONSTRAINT IF EXISTS "<live name>"` / `DROP INDEX IF EXISTS`, gated
behind `--allow-destructive`). Constraint names are read off the live object for
the drop, which is why they survive canonicalization.

Changing which columns a PRIMARY KEY covers is a replacement: the old constraint
is dropped by its real live name and the new one added, in that order, in place on
a table that already holds rows. The new key columns must already be `NOT NULL`
and unique across existing rows or Postgres rejects the `ADD` and the whole
reconcile rolls back. Generated ALTERs run with the managed schemas on
`search_path`, mirroring the DDL files.

### dbd diff

Read-only. Show the complete difference between the live database and the
design — columns, PK/unique, foreign keys, CHECK constraints, indexes, column
comments and enums, plus matview drift. It compares the same model `reconcile`
converges (table comments are in neither); diff changes nothing, works after
`dbd release`, and also shows what reconcile won't touch (orphans without
`--prune`, orphan enums, drifted matviews). Under `--scope` it refuses on a
dependency gap.

```sh
dbd diff -d $DATABASE_URL              # human report (summary + SQL)
dbd diff -d $DATABASE_URL --json       # structured diff for tooling/CI
dbd diff -d $DATABASE_URL --exit-code  # 0 in sync, 2 on drift, 1 on error
```

The desired schema is parsed from DDL, the live schema introspected; dbd
normalizes representation noise (type aliases plus array and date-time spellings
— `int4`→`integer`, `text[3]`→`text[]`, `time`→`time without time zone`; default
casts, enum qualification, PK/UNIQUE-backing indexes, FK `NO ACTION`/auto-generated
names, and CHECK-expression spelling via libpg_query — parens/case, `IN` ↔
`= ANY (ARRAY[…])`, literal casts, `BETWEEN` ↔ its `>=`/`<=` expansion, casts on
`ARRAY[…]` constructors, and `AND`/`OR` nesting) so only real drift shows. An
unparseable CHECK is shown flagged `advisory`. Covers tables + enums
structurally, plus **materialized-view drift** (each matview reported
`missing`/`drifted`/`unstamped`/`orphan` via its `dbd:hash` sentinel; in `--json`
as `matview_drift`, and counts toward `--exit-code`). Views/functions/roles/
sequences are not structurally diffed.

### dbd release (alias: dbd baseline)

Cut the first version: write a **baseline snapshot** at the current
`project.version` (the anchor future `dbd snapshot` diffs against) and set
`project.released: true`, which locks the project into the snapshot/migration
workflow and disables `dbd reconcile`.

```sh
dbd release --name "v1 GA"   # baseline snapshot + released: true
dbd baseline                 # alias
```

Refuses if the project is already released or if snapshots already exist, and if
the design has entity errors (run `dbd inspect` first). After release the flow is
the ordinary one: edit DDL → `dbd snapshot` → `dbd apply`.

**Snapshots but not released.** `init --from-db` and `merge` write snapshots
without setting `released`. Such a project is on the migration track (snapshot →
apply), still allows `reconcile`, and `release` refuses on it ("Snapshots already
exist"). Set `released: true` in `design.yaml` by hand to make reconcile refuse.

### dbd snapshot

```sh
dbd snapshot --name "add notes column"
dbd snapshot --list
```

Diffs the current DDL against the latest snapshot and writes a versioned
migration. **Smart multi-snapshot**: complex changes auto-split into safe stages —
a column rename → 2 snapshots (add+copy, drop old), a type change → 2 (add+CAST,
drop old), an enum value removal → 3 (data fix, TEXT intermediary, enum recreate).

`*.data.sql` corrections run after the matching `*.sql` (CAST heuristics auto-fill
type conversions; non-derivable cases like enum value mapping emit `-- TODO:`
comments). These are **gated**: `dbd inspect` surfaces unresolved TODOs and
`dbd apply` refuses to run while any remain.

### dbd migrate

```sh
dbd migrate --status   # read-only: local snapshot version vs database version
```

`migrate` is diagnostic only — there is no `--apply`. Pending migrations are
executed by `dbd apply` (it runs DDL + pending migrations together).

### dbd policies

```sh
dbd policies                # apply policies/<schema>/<table>.sql (RLS)
dbd policies --dry-run
dbd policies --scope hub    # only policies whose table is in the scope
dbd apply --with-policies   # apply entities + policies in one step
```

Row-Level Security policy files contain idempotent SQL (`enable row level
security`, `drop policy if exists`, `create policy`). Failures are logged and
skipped (fail-forward); exit code 1 if any failed.

`dbd deploy` (and `Design::deploy`) runs this phase unconditionally as its final
step. There, a failed policy file is a warning rather than an error: it is
reported and counted, and the deploy still exits 0.

**Scope.** A policy protects one table, and its target is read from the path —
`policies/<schema>/<table>.sql` names `<schema>.<table>`. Under `--scope`, a
policy whose table is outside the working set is skipped, with the file, target
and scope named, and counted in the deploy summary:

```
Skipped ./policies/dojo/repository_metrics.sql — dojo.repository_metrics is outside scope 'daemon'
```

This matters when one design serves several planes: without it, a policy for a
schema a plane lacks runs anyway and reports `FAILED … schema dojo does not
exist` on every deploy — an expected condition dressed as an error, which is how
real failures stop being read. Runs without `--scope` apply every file.
`dbd policies --dry-run` lists every file without the scope filter; the real run
filters.

A file off the `policies/<schema>/<table>.sql` layout has no derivable target and
always applies — scope filtering here is a correctness aid, not a security
boundary.

### dbd combine

```sh
dbd combine -f init.sql
dbd combine --scope hub -f hub.sql      # only the 'hub' scope's working set
dbd combine --scope hub --deps include  # self-contained closure
```

`--scope`/`--deps` filter the combined SQL to the working set (filter-only, no gap gate). Roles are kept in every scope; extensions too, unless the scope sets an `extensions` allowlist (`[]` ⇒ none).

### Exposed vs internal schemas

```yaml
schemas:
  - app:
      exposed: true     # PostgREST serves this
  - internal            # private (the default)
```

A table in an exposed schema is reachable by `anon` over HTTP. Internal unless
declared, except `public` on a `supabase` target. `exposed: false` overrides
that default; a bare name does not.

`dbd inspect` reports tables in exposed schemas with no RLS policy
(`policies/<schema>/<table>.sql`). Advisory — never changes the exit code.

A different axis from platform ownership: `extensions` is Supabase's and not
exposed; your own schema can be exposed without being Supabase's. Ownership
decides what `reconcile --prune` may drop; exposure decides what is readable
from outside.

### dbd emit

```sh
dbd emit --dialect mysql -f schema.mysql.sql
dbd emit --dialect tsql  -f schema.tsql.sql --report downgrades.json
dbd emit --dialect sqlite --scope hub -f hub.sqlite.sql
```

Translates the schema into **another engine's** DDL. Not `combine`, which
consolidates this project's own DDL into one script for its own target.

Targets: `mysql`, `tsql`, `sqlite`. The **source must be PostgreSQL** — it is
the only dialect dbd reads into columns and constraints, so emitting from a
T-SQL, MySQL or SQLite project is refused rather than producing an empty
schema.

Tables — columns, `NOT NULL`, defaults, primary keys, unique constraints,
foreign keys, `CHECK` constraints and indexes — and views/materialized views
(as `CREATE VIEW`, body passed through untranslated and reported). A `CHECK`
expression and an index expression or predicate are passed through untranslated
and reported, like view bodies. Functions, procedures and triggers are skipped
and reported: their bodies are PL/pgSQL or SQL that does not translate. Schemas,
extensions, roles, sequences and enum types produce no statement.

Anything the target cannot express is **downgraded to the nearest thing it
can, and reported** — never a reason to refuse the whole schema. A loss appears
as a comment at the site in the emitted file (schema folds and skipped routines
have no site, so they are in the summary and report only) and in the run's
summary. `--report <file>` writes the same set as a JSON array of
`{entity, column, from, to, reason}` so CI can assert on the count.

Mapping (⚠ = reported): `text[]`/any array → MySQL `JSON` ⚠, T-SQL
`nvarchar(max)` ⚠, SQLite `TEXT` ⚠; `jsonb` → `JSON` / `nvarchar(max)` ⚠ /
`TEXT` ⚠; `uuid` → `CHAR(36)` ⚠ / `uniqueidentifier` / `TEXT` ⚠; `timestamptz` →
`DATETIME` / `datetimeoffset` / `TEXT`; `boolean` → `TINYINT(1)` / `bit` /
`INTEGER`; an **enum** or any other type → `VARCHAR(255)` ⚠ / `nvarchar(255)` ⚠ /
`TEXT` ⚠ (MySQL `ENUM` is not used and no CHECK is added — the values are no
longer enforced). MySQL and SQLite fold the schema into the name
(`schema_table`) ⚠; T-SQL keeps `[schema].[table]`. Not reported in 0.24.1:
defaults other than literals, `now()` and booleans are dropped; serial/identity
columns lose auto-increment; generated columns lose their expression.

```sql
-- dbd: `tags` was `text[]` — emitted as JSON; no array type exists here, so
--      the `text` elements become a JSON document
`tags` JSON,
```

A *faithful* mapping is not reported. `integer` → `INT` loses nothing, and a
report padded with those is one nobody reads.

The exit status stays 0 when downgrades happen — they are the documented
behaviour, not a failure — which is why the count is what a pipeline should
assert on.

### dbd graph

```sh
dbd graph
dbd graph -n config.lookups             # subgraph from one entity
dbd graph --scope hub                    # filter to the 'hub' scope (composes with -n)
```

Output: `{ "nodes": [...], "edges": [...], "layers": [...], "scope": "hub" | null }`.
`scope` (v0.12.0+) names the scope the graph was narrowed to, `null` when
unscoped — in the JSON rather than beside it, since stdout is a contract here.
The other scope-filtering commands (`dbml`, `combine`, `export`) print
`scope '<name>': <kept> of <total> entities`; unscoped runs print nothing.

### dbd diagram

```sh
dbd diagram                        # build the model and open the hosted interactive viewer
dbd diagram --print-url            # print the viewer URL instead of opening a browser
dbd diagram --site http://localhost:5173   # point at a different site (or set $DBD_DIAGRAM_URL)
dbd diagram --scope hub            # scope-aware (only the scope's tables/refs)
dbd diagram --json -f schema.json  # write the raw SchemaModel JSON for upload/tooling
```

Opens the hosted interactive viewer at `https://dbd.sensei-hq.com/diagram` (root tabs Overview / Diagram / Entities (tables) / Changelog; per entity Details / Diagram / Changelog, enums Details / Changelog; a sidebar of every entity — tables, views, matviews, functions, procedures, triggers, enums — searchable and filterable by type — tables with fields, references, dependencies, a relationship diagram and their own changelog; views and routines with what they use and what uses them; enums with their values). The dbd-native schema model (schemas/tables/columns/FK refs) is gzip-compressed into the URL fragment — client-side only, never sent to a server, so the link is private and self-contained. `--print-url` prints the link without opening a browser (useful on headless machines). `--site`/`$DBD_DIAGRAM_URL` overrides the base URL. `--json -f schema.json` writes the raw SchemaModel JSON; drag the file onto the site's `/diagram` page (no file picker) or feed it to other tooling. The viewer keeps the designs you open in the browser's localStorage (`dbd:diagram:<project>`, listed and removable at `/projects`); nothing is sent to a server. The model carries `version` (currently `3`) and, being JSON rather than DBML, covers more than tables: `tables` (columns with `pk`/`nn`/`en`/`fk`/`uq`, type, default, comment, plus indexes), `refs` (foreign keys — the ER edges, column-level as `{s,t,c}`), `entities` (views, materialized views, functions, procedures, triggers — triggers come from the T-SQL/MySQL readers), `deps` (what reads/writes/calls what — the call graph), and `schemas`/`project`. `entities`/`deps` are deliberately separate from `tables`/`refs`: an ER renderer wants FKs, a call-graph renderer wants dependencies, and folding them would change what every existing consumer of `tables` receives. A dep edge whose target is not a project entity (a built-in like `now()`, or a dangling reference) is marked `"unresolved": true` rather than dropped — the edge is real, only the endpoint is unplaceable. Comments reach the model for every kind, not just tables: `note` is the first line, `noteMd` the full text. `history` (v3, omitted when there are no snapshots) is what each snapshot changed, oldest first: the first a `baseline` of table/enum counts, each later one the tables and enums it added, removed or modified with their column, index, constraint and enum-value edits; a multi-stage rename or type change is one entry spanning `version`..`through` and reads as the rename or type change; type spellings are canonicalised; views and routines have no history (snapshots hold tables and enums only); under `--scope` it covers the scope's entities only. `enums` (v3, omitted when there are none) carries each enum type with its values in declaration order and its comment.

### dbd dbml

```sh
dbd dbml                       # writes design.dbml (when no dbml keys configured)
dbd dbml -f schema.dbml        # custom path; multi-doc keeps the directory, replaces filename
dbd dbml --scope hub -f hub.dbml      # document only the 'hub' scope's working set
dbd dbml --scope hub --deps include   # expand to the dependency closure first
```

When `design.yaml` declares multiple `dbml.<key>` entries, `dbd dbml` writes one file per key into the parent directory of `-f`, using each key's `output` (default `<key>.dbml`).

`--scope`/`--deps` are honored: the generated DBML covers the scope's working set (the closure under `deps: include`, the plain selection under `report`). `dbml` documents rather than deploys, so it does not gate on dependency gaps — out-of-scope FK targets still render as external stub tables.

Per-doc options:

| Field | Type | Effect |
|-------|------|--------|
| `include.schemas` / `include.tables` | list | Only matching entities appear in this doc |
| `exclude.schemas` / `exclude.tables` | list | Removes matching entities |
| `output` | string | Output filename; default `<key>.dbml` |
| `auto_group_by_schema` | bool | Emit `TableGroup <schema>` for every schema in the filtered set |
| `groups` | list of `{name, tables}` | Explicit `TableGroup` blocks; names take precedence over auto-by-schema |

```yaml
dbml:
  base:
    exclude: { schemas: [staging] }
    auto_group_by_schema: true
    output: design.dbml
  core:
    include: { schemas: [config] }
    output: core.dbml
    groups:
      - name: lookups
        tables: [config.lookups, config.lookup_values]
```

Composite foreign keys (multi-column inline or table-level `ForeignKey`) emit DBML tuple syntax: `Ref: "schema"."table".("c1", "c2") > "schema"."other".("c1", "c2") [delete: cascade]`.

### dbd format

River-style DDL formatter. Operates on all `*.ddl` files in the project tree.

```sh
dbd format                     # rewrite files in place
dbd format --check             # exit 1 if any file would change (CI / pre-commit)
```

Driven by the optional `format:` section in `design.yaml` (falls back to defaults when absent):

```yaml
format:
  keyword_case: lower          # lower | upper | preserve
  comma_style: leading         # leading | trailing
  type_alignment: 27           # column for type start, 0 = off
  indent: 2
  query_style: river           # river (default) | none
  gutter: 10                   # river: width of right-aligned keyword column
```

`query_style: river` (the default) right-aligns keywords at `gutter`, leading-comma SELECT lists, alias/operator alignment, one condition per line. It applies to CREATE VIEW bodies + standalone SELECTs. **Safety:** river output is only used if it re-parses to the same AST as the source; any query the renderer can't reproduce faithfully (CTEs, etc.) falls back to keyword-case-only — the formatter never changes SQL semantics. Set `query_style: none` to disable river.

The splitter understands two atomic-body kinds: PG `$$ ... $$` blocks (function bodies) and SQLite `CREATE TRIGGER ... BEGIN ... END;` blocks. CASE expressions inside trigger bodies are handled correctly — only `END;` at a word boundary closes the block.

#### Pre-commit integration

`.pre-commit-hooks.yaml` at the repo root exposes two hooks:

- `dbd-format` — `language: rust`; pre-commit clones the repo at the pinned `rev`, runs
  `cargo install --path .`, caches afterward. **Needs v0.12.3 or later**: earlier tags
  have a virtual manifest at the repo root, so that install aborts with `found a virtual
  manifest instead of a package manifest` during environment setup, before anything is
  formatted. Use `dbd-format-system` with an older `rev`.
- `dbd-format-system` — `language: system`; expects `dbd` already on PATH (`cargo install
  dbd-cli`). Works at any `rev`.

Both set `pass_filenames: false` because `dbd format` scans the project itself. Consumers add to their `.pre-commit-config.yaml`:

```yaml
- repo: https://github.com/sensei-hq/dbd
  rev: v0.24.1
  hooks:
    - id: dbd-format
```

### dbd reset

Guarded by the bookkeeping environment check (`dbd.meta` on Postgres/Supabase, `_dbd_meta` on SQLite) **and** the scope guard (a wrong-`--scope` reset is refused unless `--allow-scope-change` or `--force`; see [dbd apply](#dbd-apply)). **Entity-level by default**: drops the
project's own objects individually — functions/procedures (every overload via a
`DROP ROUTINE` DO-block), materialized views (`DROP MATERIALIZED VIEW … CASCADE`,
before the views/tables they read), views, tables, sequences, enums — in reverse
dependency order. Never `DROP SCHEMA`/`DROP EXTENSION` by default, so `public`, custom schemas
and extensions (e.g. pgvector) survive and never abort on `public`; the next `apply`
repopulates the schemas.

```sh
dbd reset                    # Blocked if prod or version >= 1
dbd reset --force            # Override guard
dbd reset --dry-run
dbd reset --schemas          # also DROP SCHEMA for managed schemas
dbd reset --extensions       # also DROP EXTENSION for configured extensions
dbd reset --clean            # = --schemas --extensions
dbd reset --target postgres  # protected-schema set (default: the design's target key)
dbd reset --scope hub --dry-run   # only the objects the 'hub' scope occupies
```

`--target <postgres|supabase>` selects which schemas are protected from `DROP SCHEMA` under
`--schemas`. It defaults to the design's target key (the first `target:` entry), so a Supabase
project is protected without the flag; on `supabase` the managed set (`public`, `auth`,
`storage`, `realtime`, `graphql_public`, `supabase_functions`, `pgbouncer`, `pgsodium`, `vault`,
`extensions`, `supabase_migrations`) is skipped; on `postgres` `public` is dropped, and the
target's roles are dropped on a full reset. The guards read the database: refused when it is
marked prod (rows written as `production` included) or at version ≥ 1, unless `--force`;
`--dry-run` needs no connection and checks no guard.

`--schemas` additionally `DROP SCHEMA … CASCADE`s the managed schemas, always skipping
`pg_catalog`/`information_schema`/`pg_toast`; on a `supabase` target also skipping the
Supabase set (`auth`, `storage`, …, `public`), while on `postgres` `public` is dropped.
`--extensions` `DROP EXTENSION … CASCADE`s each extension in the target's `extensions:`
config. `--clean` = both. `--scope` restricts the reset to the objects (and, with
`--schemas`, the schemas) the scope's working set occupies; roles are dropped only on a
full reset (no `--scope`).

### dbd doctor

```sh
dbd doctor
dbd doctor --fix
```

Audits + migrates: old Node.js `design.yaml` format → new format (`--fix` writes a `.yaml.bak`); removes stale internally-managed files; migrates plural DDL type folders to singular (`ddl/functions/` → `ddl/function/`, merging into an existing singular folder, backing up the older file on a same-name collision as `<name>.ddl.bkp`). Also reports **misfiled view DDL** — a `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW` under `ddl/view/` (which makes `reset` emit `DROP VIEW` on it) or a plain view under `ddl/materialized_view/` — with a move hint; `--fix` does not move these. Always exits 0.

---

### dbd install

```sh
dbd install                # install globally into ~/.claude (skills/ + agents/)
dbd install --project      # install into the current project's ./.claude instead
dbd install --dry-run      # preview what would be written, touch nothing
```

Installs dbd's Claude Code assets — the `dbd` skill (`skills/dbd/SKILL.md`) and the `dbd-pattern-verifier` agent (`agents/dbd-pattern-verifier.md`) — so an AI assistant working in the project understands the schema-as-code conventions. The assets are embedded in the binary, so this needs no repo checkout or network access.

Two scopes, and neither is system-wide (all OS users): **global** (default) writes under `$CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` if set, else `~/.claude`, and is personal to your machine across every project; **`--project`** writes `./.claude` (relative to `--source`), which is shared with the team only once you commit that directory (gitignore it to keep the install local to your checkout). Each asset is reported as created, updated, or unchanged — an overwrite on upgrade is never silent — and re-running is idempotent. Restart Claude Code afterwards to load the new skill/agent.

---

## GitHub source

`dbd deploy` is the only command that takes a GitHub source. Every other command
refuses one with a message — clone the repository and pass its local path.

```sh
# Shorthand
dbd deploy --source sensei-hq/daemon/database -d $DATABASE_URL

# With branch/tag
dbd deploy --source sensei-hq/daemon/database@v2.1 -d $DATABASE_URL

# Full URL
dbd deploy --source https://github.com/owner/repo/tree/main/database -d $DATABASE_URL

# GitHub downloads are cached under ~/.cache/dbd (macOS: ~/Library/Caches/dbd),
# keyed by owner-repo-ref and reused while a design.yaml is present.
# dbd deploy --no-cache re-downloads the current source;
# dbd deploy --clear-cache wipes the entire cache directory first.
```

For a private repository set `GITHUB_TOKEN`: dbd sends it as a bearer token to
`api.github.com` and nowhere else.

---

## Library usage

The guide page *Embedding dbd-core* (https://dbd.sensei-hq.com/guide/embedding)
covers the whole API; every example there is compiled by the test suite.
`Design::deploy` applies the configured grants like `dbd deploy`.
`Design::reconcile` does not check `project.released` — callers must.
`history::load_scoped(project_dir, keep)` takes a `keep(schema, name) -> bool`
predicate.

```rust
use dbd_core::{connect, ApplyComplete, Design};
use dbd_core::design::Progress;
use std::path::Path;

// Load the declarative design for an environment (sync; scans ddl/ next to the config).
let mut design = Design::from_config(Path::new("design.yaml"), "prod")?;

// Inspection — offline, no database. (`report` takes &mut self: it caches validation.)
let report = design.report(None, None);
// report.issues:              errors blocking the active scope (what apply refuses on)
// report.out_of_scope_issues: errored entities the scope excludes (non-blocking)
// report.warnings:            entities with warnings
// report.gaps:                out-of-scope dependency gaps (when a scope is passed)

// Connect an adapter — Postgres/SQLite/Convex is chosen from the URL scheme.
let adapter = connect("postgres://localhost/mydb", &design.config().project.name).await?;

// Resolve the scope once (None, None ⇒ full design, the scope's default deps policy).
let scope = design.resolve_scope(None, None)?;

// apply / import_data take FIVE arguments: (&*adapter, name, dry_run, scope,
// progress). The three callbacks travel together in one `Progress` value —
// on_start(&str), on_done(&str, Option<&str>), on_complete(summary) — they are
// NOT three separate arguments. `Progress::none()` for a silent run.
// deploy drops the name and takes on_complete directly: (&*adapter, dry_run,
// scope, on_complete(DeployComplete)).
design
    .apply(&*adapter, None, /*dry_run*/ false, Some(&scope), Progress {
        on_start: |desc: &str| println!("→ {desc}"),
        on_done: |desc: &str, err: Option<&str>| if let Some(e) = err { eprintln!("✗ {desc}: {e}") },
        on_complete: |s: ApplyComplete| println!("applied {} entities", s.applied),
    })
    .await?;
design.import_data(&*adapter, None, false, Some(&scope), Progress::none()).await?;

// Or apply + import + policies in one call — the same pipeline `dbd deploy`
// runs, so an embedder and the CLI cannot drift. A failed policy file does not
// fail the deploy; it lands in s.policies.failed and in s.warnings().
design.deploy(&*adapter, false, Some(&scope), |s| {
    println!("v{} — {} table(s) imported", s.apply.to_version, s.import.tables);
    for w in s.warnings() { eprintln!("warning: {w}"); }
}).await?;
// Use design.deploy_with_progress(&*adapter, dry_run, scope, Progress { .. })
// for per-step callbacks (spinner / logging).

// Dependency graph (for visualization) — returns Result.
let graph = design.graph(None, None)?;
// graph.nodes, graph.edges, graph.layers
```

---

## Targets

| Target | Adapter | URL form | Extensions | Roles | SQL exec | Import | Migrations |
|--------|---------|----------|------------|-------|----------|--------|------------|
| PostgreSQL | sqlx-postgres | `postgres://user:pass@host:5432/db` | yes | yes | yes | COPY streaming (CSV/TSV/JSONL) | `dbd.migrations` (dedicated `dbd` schema) |
| Supabase | sqlx-postgres (same adapter; the `supabase` key exposes `public`, protects Supabase schemas from prune/reset, adds PostgREST grants) | `postgres://…` (with `target: supabase`) | yes | yes | yes | COPY streaming | `dbd.migrations` (dedicated `dbd` schema) |
| SQLite | sqlx-sqlite | `sqlite://./app.db`, `sqlite::memory:`, `file:/abs/path` | no (errors) | no (errors) | yes | multi-row `INSERT ... VALUES (?,?),(?,?), ...` batches in one tx (CSV/TSV/JSONL) | `_dbd_migrations` (SQLite syntax) |
| Convex | codegen | `convex:` (→ `./convex`), `convex://./out`, append `?deploy=true` to auto-deploy | no (errors) | no (errors) | no — `apply` writes `<dir>/schema.ts` | per-table via `npx convex import --table <name> --replace -y <file>`; whole-deployment export via `npx convex export` (CLI has no per-table flag) | sidecar `<dir>/.dbd_state.json` |
| MySQL / SQL Server | **none** — `mysql://`, `mariadb://`, `sqlserver://`, `mssql://` refused by name | — | — | — | — | — | — |

### Adapter quirks

- **SQLite**: no schemas — `Schema` entities are silently no-op; entity names like `auth.users` resolve to the bare table `users` via `sqlite_master`. `Enum`/`Function`/`Procedure`/`Role`/`Extension`/`Sequence`/`MaterializedView` are rejected at apply time. No transactional apply; grants skipped; policy files fail; a SQLite project (`verbatim` reader) cannot `diff`/`reconcile`/`emit`.
    - **Offline ref classifier** — `classify_reference` checks an alphabetically sorted table of ~150 built-ins (aggregates, window/math/date/JSON1/scalar functions, type names) via `binary_search`, plus a `sqlite_*` prefix rule that catches all reserved system tables/views (`sqlite_master`, `sqlite_sequence`, `sqlite_stat1`, …). Everything else falls through to `UserDefined`.
    - **Trigger-aware DDL splitter** — `dbd format`'s statement splitter recognises SQLite `CREATE TRIGGER … BEGIN <stmts;> END;` blocks and keeps them atomic. `BEGIN` is only treated as trigger-body when the in-flight block already contains the `TRIGGER` keyword, so bare `BEGIN; … COMMIT;` transactions still split correctly. `CASE … END` inside the body doesn't trip the close detector — only `END` immediately followed by `;` at a word boundary closes the block.
    - **Batched imports** — `import_delimited` and `import_jsonl` flush rows in multi-row `INSERT … VALUES (?,?),(?,?), …` batches sized by `batch_row_size(col_count) = min(500, 32000 / col_count)`. CSV uses a fixed header; JSONL detects per-line column-set changes and flushes the previous group before starting a new one. All inside a single transaction per import.
- **Convex**: codegen, not a SQL engine — `execute_script` returns an error (so `reset`, `policies`, grants, `diff` and `reconcile` are unavailable); only tables and enums are written, other entity types are skipped without a message; `apply_entities` is the canonical path (`prefers_batch_apply() = true`). Table names flatten `schema.entity` → `schema_entity` (Convex disallows `.`). SQL → Convex validator: `int*`/`numeric` → `v.number()`, text-like (`text`/`varchar`/`uuid`/`citext`) → `v.string()`, `boolean` → `v.boolean()`, timestamps → `v.number()` (epoch ms), `jsonb`/`json` → `v.any()`, `bytea`/`blob` → `v.bytes()`, `T[]` → `v.array(T)`, nullable → `v.optional(T)`. Indexes emit as `.index("name", ["col"])`. Convex platform columns `_id` / `_creationTime` are skipped if present.
    - **Enums** — an `Entity::Enum` named `config.status` with values `[active, inactive]` emits
      `export const config_status = v.union(v.literal("active"), v.literal("inactive"));` above
      `defineSchema`. Column whose `data_type` matches either the qualified name (`config.status`)
      or the bare name (`status`, case-insensitive) routes to that const; arrays become
      `v.array(config_status)`; nullable columns wrap in `v.optional(...)`.
    - **Foreign keys** — single-column inline FKs (`ColumnDef.inline_fk`) and single-column
      table-level `TableConstraint::ForeignKey` whose target is a known table emit
      `<col>: v.id("target_convex_name")` (with `v.optional(...)` wrapping for nullable
      columns). Composite/multi-column FKs fall back to the scalar validator since Convex
      `v.id` only addresses one table.
    - **Auto-deploy** — `convex://./out?deploy=true` (or `ConvexAdapter::with_auto_deploy(true)`)
      runs `npx convex deploy` from the parent of the schema directory after `apply_entities`
      writes the file. Skipped when there were no entities to apply.
    - **Import** — `import_data(entity, dry_run)` shells out to
      `npx convex import --table <flat_name> --replace -y <file>`. `dry_run = true` logs
      the command and returns Ok without spawning.
    - **CLI dry-run** — `ConvexAdapter::with_cli_dry_run(true)` short-circuits all
      `npx convex …` invocations (deploy + import) to a stderr log line. Used in tests and by
      `dbd apply --dry-run` to avoid touching a live deployment.

---

## Reference cache (offline `inspect`)

`dbd inspect --from-db` runs `adapter.list_entities()` against the live database (via the `-d`/`--database` connection) — pulling every user-defined table, view, and enum (system schemas excluded) — and writes the snapshot to `<project>/.dbd/refcache.json`:

```json
{
  "captured_at": "2026-05-15T12:34:56Z",
  "source": "postgres",
  "entities": ["auth.users", "public.lookups", "config.user_role"]
}
```

Subsequent runs of `dbd inspect` (no `--from-db`, no `DATABASE_URL` needed) load this snapshot and drop any "Unresolved reference: NAME" warning whose target is in the set. Useful for CI, offline editing, or when the database is temporarily down. Commit the file to share with the team, or `.gitignore` it for purely local use.

API: `Design::write_ref_cache(adapter, source)` / `Design::resolve_unknown_refs_via_cache()` / `RefCache::{load,save,contains}` in `dbd_core::refcache`.

---

## Safety model

The bookkeeping table records project name, environment, and version. On Postgres/Supabase this is
`dbd.meta` in a dedicated `dbd` schema (paired with `dbd.migrations`); the `dbd` schema is not in
PostgREST's default `db-schemas` (so it's unreachable via the API), and it's excluded from
reverse-engineering/`merge`/DBML/`diagram`/introspection and protected from `dbd reset`
(`--schemas`/`--clean` never drop it). Existing databases heal automatically — on the next
`apply`/`deploy`/`reconcile`/`reset`, dbd relocates legacy `public._dbd_meta`/`public._dbd_migrations`
(and any scoped-apply strays in other schemas) into `dbd.meta`/`dbd.migrations` and drops the
originals; no user action required. On SQLite it's `_dbd_meta`/`_dbd_migrations` (SQLite has no
schemas, so the prefix is the namespace). Convex keeps migrations + meta in a JSON sidecar next to
`schema.ts`.

| State | `reset` | `reset --force` |
|-------|---------|-----------------|
| dev, version 0 | allowed | allowed |
| dev, version >= 1 | blocked | allowed |
| prod (or a legacy `production` row), any version | blocked | allowed |
| fresh (no table) | allowed | allowed |

The environment is the one recorded by the last write — `-e` defaults to `prod`,
so a database applied without `-e dev` is prod.

---

## Environment variables

| Variable | Used by |
|----------|---------|
| `DATABASE_URL` | Default database connection — overrides `target.url`, overridden by `-d` |
| `$NAME` in `target.url` | A whole-value `url: $NAME` is read from the environment (unset ⇒ used literally) |
| `GITHUB_TOKEN` | `dbd deploy` from a private GitHub repo — sent as a bearer token to `api.github.com` only |
| `DBD_DIAGRAM_URL` | Base URL `dbd diagram` opens (default `https://dbd.sensei-hq.com`); `--site` overrides |
| `DBD_NO_TX` | Set (any value) to apply without the single transaction |
| `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` | Global install dir for `dbd install` (default `~/.claude`) |

The GitHub download cache is the platform cache dir + `/dbd`
(`$XDG_CACHE_HOME` or `~/.cache` on Linux, `~/Library/Caches` on macOS).

---

## Access control

Grants come from `schemas[].grants` and the first target's `grants` (any key),
merged per schema; applied by `dbd apply` and `dbd deploy` after the schema;
`usage` → schema USAGE, other perms → `ON ALL TABLES` + default privileges; plus
`NOTIFY pgrst`. Config grants cover schemas and tables — grant on functions or
sequences in an `apply.after` hook. On a `supabase` target, configured grants add
USAGE for `anon`/`authenticated`/`service_role` on every listed schema.
`exposed:` grants nothing; it drives `inspect`'s advisory "No RLS policy on N
table(s) in exposed schema(s)" report. RLS policies (`policies/<schema>/<table>.sql`):
`deploy` always (failure = warning, exit 0), `dbd policies` and
`apply --with-policies` (failure = exit 1), plain `apply` never.

## Other dialects and encodings

Readers: `pg_query` (PostgreSQL; structured), `tsql` and `mysql` (statement heads:
identity + references, no columns; the only readers that report triggers),
`verbatim` (SQLite: the file is the model). A T-SQL/MySQL project can `inspect`,
`graph` and `combine`; `diff`/`reconcile`/`emit` refuse; `dbml`/`diagram` show no
tables; `snapshot` records nothing; there is no adapter to apply to. DDL files
are decoded from UTF-8, or UTF-8/UTF-16LE/UTF-16BE with a byte-order mark; no mark
and not UTF-8 is an error naming the file. Caveat in 0.24.1: `apply`/`deploy`/
`combine` read the SQL they execute without that decoding, so a UTF-16 file is
skipped when applied — re-encode it as UTF-8.
